To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) Two-photon excitation microscopy allows the visualization of dendritic [Ca(2+)] transients in vivo.
dendrites of pyramidal neurons are not active and do not generate action potentials in response to sensory stimuli in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of dendritic calcium in the processing of information in pyramidal neurons.
how the nervous system processes information and how this is reflected in the electrical activity of neurons.
the role of the dendritic tree as a site for the integration of sensory input.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ca2+ action potential propagation in dendrites is a rare event in vivo.
dendritic Na+ action potentials are generated and propagate in an all or none fashion in the intact brain, but that Ca2+ action potential propagation is limited to the proximal apices.

dendritic Na+ action potentials are triggered by somatically generated Na+ action potentials, and Ca2+ transients in the apical dendritic tree are generated by somatically generated dendritic Na+ spikes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dendrites of neocortical neurons do not support Ca2+ action potential generation, but are sites of Ca2+ entry during back-propagating Na+ action potentials and are therefore likely to be important sites of Ca2+-dependent synaptic plasticity.
the dendritic Ca2+ dynamics in the neocortical neurons are mainly determined by somatic action potential.

dendrites of pyramidal neurons in vivo can generate Na+ spikes and Ca2+ spikes, which are initiated at the soma and propagate in the dendritic tree, and that the Ca2+ transients in the dendrites are proportional to the number and location of Na+ spikes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons do not generate Ca2+-action potentials.
dendrites of neocortical neurons can be studied in vivo, and that this is a powerful tool for the study of neuronal function in the intact brain.
dendrites are not passive conduits for synaptic information, but are actively involved in processing and integrating synaptic information.
